name: chapel
desc: Programming language for productive parallel computing at scale
why: A parallel programming language from Cray with a global-view model that is a strange and rarely explored corner of language design.

brief.what_it_is: Chapel is a compiled, open-source programming language for parallel computing, aimed at code that runs from a laptop up to clusters and supercomputers. You write one program using Chapel's parallel constructs (such as coforall, forall, and on loc) and the compiler turns it into machine code. The same language features also cover GPU execution and running across multiple compute nodes ('locales'). The homepage shows small examples: Hello World, Distributed Hello World, parallel file IO, a 1D heat diffusion solver, and a GPU kernel. The brew caveats describe running multi-locale programs locally and simulating a GPU with --gpu=cpu.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says Chapel is designed for productive parallel computing at scale and is meant to run on the CPUs and GPUs of laptops, desktops, commodity clusters, and the cloud, as well as the high-end supercomputers it was built for. The homepage tagline is 'Productive parallel computing at every scale.'
brief.how_it_works: The homepage says Chapel is a compiled language that generates efficient machine code. Parallelism is expressed with language constructs: coforall creates a task per core, forall runs iterations in parallel, and on loc moves work to a compute node. The homepage says GPU programming uses the same language features as distributed execution, with no separate API. Beyond that, the pages I read did not explain the internals.

brief.install_notes: Homebrew is one of several routes: brew update, then brew install chapel, and CHPL_HOME can be found with chpl --print-chpl-home. The download page also lists building from source (chapel-2.10.0.tar.gz on GitHub, then the Quickstart instructions), Spack (variants replace the usual CHPL_* environment settings), a Docker image, prebuilt Linux packages for many distributions (RHEL-family systems need EPEL first), and 'module load chapel' on HPE Cray EX systems. No accounts or licences are needed beyond the open-source install. Multi-locale and GPU runs need the extra compile flags in the brew caveats.
brief.standout: Most languages with a parallel story use a library or a separate GPU API; Chapel tries to express distributed multi-node execution and GPU kernels with the same language constructs, using a global-view style where you write over whole arrays and domains and the 'on' clauses decide placement. The homepage example for distributed array iteration uses blockDist, and the GPU example uses here.gpus with on gpu. The scout note calls it a rarely explored corner of language design, and the homepage claims code that is shorter than C/OpenMP predecessors (the CHAMPS case).
brief.status: Maintained. The homepage's latest news item is 'Announcing Chapel 2.10!' dated September 24, 2026, and the download page names 2.10.0 as the current version. The homepage also lists news posts from April to September 2026, and the download page links prebuilt packages for many distributions. I did not check commit history or the release page.
brief.caveats: By default, compiled Chapel programs run only on a single locale; multi-locale and GPU simulation need the extra compile flags from the brew caveats. Download page caveats: BigInteger performance and the bundled GASNet multi-locale builds need a source build for best results, and the bundled libfabric multi-locale configuration is experimental and was known to work only with the tcp and efa providers. The HPE page says that only HPE Cray EX systems get the module load route, and other HPE or Cray systems need a source build. The README says third-party packages are under their own licences. The scout note's claim that Chapel comes from Cray is not confirmed by the pages I fetched, although the HPE Cray material is consistent with it. The homepage was reachable, so this is not an outage case.
